t.the sundarbans@22.0,89.2:
No road reaches this point. The forest is crossed only by water, and any visit here means leaving the motorcycle behind and taking a boat.

The Sundarbans is home to the Bengal tiger, which has adapted to life in the mangroves, swimming between islands and hunting deer, wild boar and fish. Tigers here have a fearsome reputation, and attacks on honey collectors, woodcutters and fishermen are a real danger. The forest is also home to saltwater crocodiles, river dolphins, spotted deer and hundreds of species of birds. Both the Bangladeshi and Indian parts of the Sundarbans are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and they protect a unique ecosystem that also shields the coast from cyclones and storm surges.

Getting to the edge of the Sundarbans by road is possible. In Bangladesh, the town of Mongla, a port on the Pasur river, and the city of Khulna further north are the usual starting points for boat trips into the forest. The roads in this part of Bangladesh are busy, with buses, trucks, rickshaws and pedestrians, and driving is chaotic by European standards. Floods during the monsoon, from June to September, can make roads impassable, and cyclones can strike in spring and autumn. The best time to visit is the dry winter season, from November to February.

Boat trips into the Sundarbans, often lasting several days, are organised by tour operators in Khulna and Mongla, and permits are required. Fuel and services are available in the towns, but nothing inside the forest. Bengali food is rich and spicy, with fish curries, rice and lentils, and the sweets are famous. Gliding along a quiet creek at dawn, with the mangroves on both sides and the mud printed with the tracks of animals, is an unforgettable experience, even if the tiger stays hidden.
t.sundarbans national park@21.9,88.9:
Let's be straight about it from the start: nobody rides a motorcycle into the Sundarbans. The national park is a maze of tidal channels, mudbanks and mangrove islands at the bottom of the Ganges–Brahmaputra delta, and the last solid tarmac gives out at the jetties around Gosaba and the villages beyond Canning. The ride is about getting to the edge of the land, parking the bike in a village yard, and stepping onto a wooden boat for the part that matters.

The run down from Kolkata is flat, hot and busy, a long ribbon of road through paddy fields, fish ponds and brick kilns, with buses that treat the centre line as a suggestion. Leave before dawn and you get the soft light over the water hyacinth and the cooler air before the humidity settles in. The last stretches narrow to embankment roads barely wider than a cart, with ponds on both sides and children waving from every doorstep. Fill the tank in Canning or the bigger roadside towns on the way; after that, fuel is sold out of bottles if at all.

What waits on the water is one of the strangest landscapes in Asia. The mangroves take their local name from the sundari tree, and the forest breathes through spiky aerial roots that poke up out of the mud at low tide. Twice a day the sea pushes in and the whole place changes shape. This is the home of the Bengal tiger in a setting no other tiger shares, swimming between islands and living on fish, crabs, deer and wild boar. You are far more likely to see a crocodile basking on a bank, a monitor lizard, kingfishers by the dozen and spotted deer at the treeline than the cat itself, and that is fine.

People here live alongside the forest in a way that will stay with you. Honey collectors, fishermen and crab catchers go into the mangroves knowing the risk, and before they do, many pray to Bonbibi, the forest goddess honoured by Hindus and Muslims alike, who is said to protect those who enter with respect and take only what they need. The national park and its wider delta were inscribed by UNESCO in 1987, and the Indian side runs into the even larger Bangladeshi Sundarbans across the border.

Go between November and February, when the air is drier and the boats run comfortably. Bring water, sunscreen and patience, arrange the boat and the permits through a registered operator, and leave the bike somewhere you trust. The ride back, with mud on your boots and the smell of salt and diesel still in your nose, feels like rejoining a different century.
t.kolkata@22.6,88.4:
Kolkata is the city that was once the capital of British India, and it still carries itself with the air of a place that remembers. The great colonial buildings, the Victoria Memorial of white marble, the Writers' Building and the High Court, stand beside the Hooghly river, and trams, the only ones still running in India, clatter along the streets. The Howrah Bridge, a huge cantilever of steel opened in 1943, carries a river of people and vehicles across the water every day, and it is held together with rivets rather than nuts and bolts.

Kolkata has more than four million people in its core and many more in the suburbs, and it is famous for its culture. College Street holds one of the biggest second-hand book markets in the world, the coffee houses are full of arguments about poetry and politics, and the festival of Durga Puja, each autumn, transforms the city with elaborate tableaux and lights. Fish, sweets and street food are central to daily life, and the sweet shops are a treat.

The ride south, toward the Sundarbans, leaves the city through crowded streets and then slows into a flat delta landscape of rice fields, ponds and villages. The Sundarbans, a vast mangrove forest at the mouth of the Ganges, is home to the Bengal tiger, saltwater crocodiles and many birds, and it is reached by boat from small landing stages. The roads are narrow, often broken, and shared with rickshaws, bicycles and buses, and distances take longer than they should. Fuel is reliable in Kolkata and the larger towns, but scarce in the delta.

The heat from April to June is heavy, and the monsoon brings flooding, so the best months are November to February. Expect to move slowly, and give yourself time. The city is a place to eat, talk and wander, and an evening on the riverbank with a cup of sweet tea is a good way to end the day.
t.sundarbans west wildlife sanctuary@21.8,:
The Sundarbans is the largest mangrove forest in the world, a vast maze of tidal rivers, creeks and muddy islands where the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers meet the Bay of Bengal. The western sanctuary, in the south west of Bangladesh close to the Indian border, is one of the protected cores of this immense wetland, part of the World Heritage listing shared between Bangladesh and India. It is the home of the Bengal tiger, which has adapted to life in the mangroves, swimming between islands and hunting in the tidal forest, as well as spotted deer, saltwater crocodiles, river dolphins and a remarkable variety of birds.

Let us be honest about one thing: this is not a place you reach by motorcycle. There are no roads into the sanctuary, and the nearest towns are far away across the water. Access is by boat only, usually on organised trips from Khulna or the port of Mongla, and visitors need permits from the Forest Department and must travel with authorised guides and guards. A ride here really means riding to the edge of the delta and then leaving the bike behind for a few days on the water.

That journey to the edge is an experience in itself. The roads of south west Bangladesh are crowded with buses, trucks, rickshaws, bicycles and livestock, and driving is chaotic by European standards, demanding patience and nerve. The landscape is flat, green and watery, with rice fields, shrimp farms, villages and rivers crossed by ferries and bridges. Fuel is available in the towns, but quality and supply can vary.

Once on the water, the Sundarbans reveals itself slowly. The boat glides along wide channels between walls of mangrove trees, their roots rising from the mud like spikes, and the silence is broken by birdsong, the splash of fish and the occasional alarm call of a deer. Tigers are rarely seen, but their presence is felt everywhere, in footprints on the mud and in the warnings of the guards. The forest also sustains local people, who collect honey, fish and wood at real risk. The best time to visit is from November to February, when the weather is cooler and drier, and the cyclone season has passed.
t.sundarbans south sanctuary@21.8,89.4:
Down at the very bottom of Bangladesh, where the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers break into countless channels before meeting the Bay of Bengal, lies the largest mangrove forest on Earth. The Sundarbans South Sanctuary is one of three protected wildlife sanctuaries in the Bangladeshi part of the forest, and the whole area is a World Heritage Site. This is a world of water and tide: creeks, rivers and islands thick with sundari trees, from which the forest may take its name, along with gewa, keora and golpata palms, all standing on breathing roots that poke up through the mud.

It is also one of the last strongholds of the Bengal tiger, which has adapted to swimming between islands and living on fish, crabs and deer. Spotted deer, wild boar, monkeys, saltwater crocodiles, river dolphins and an extraordinary range of birds, including kingfishers of several kinds, share the forest. People live with the tigers here too: honey collectors, woodcutters and fishermen work the edges and the creeks, and their prayers to Bonbibi, the forest goddess, show how seriously the danger is taken. Cyclones regularly sweep in from the Bay, and the mangroves act as a vital shield for the land behind.

Let us be honest about the riding: there is none. The forest has no roads, and the sanctuaries can only be visited by boat with a permit and an organised guide, usually from Mongla or Khulna, and trips often last two or three days. The ride part of the journey ends on the mainland, on flat, crowded roads through rice paddies, shrimp ponds and villages, where you share the tarmac with cycle rickshaws, buses and trucks. The light over the water at dawn and dusk is unforgettable, but the humidity and monsoon rains from June to September make the cool, dry winter months the time to go.

Khulna, the regional city, has fuel, hotels and supplies, and Mongla, the port town on the Pasur river, is the usual departure point for boats. Expect simple food on board: rice, lentils, fish curries and plenty of sweet tea. Bring insect repellent, sun protection and patience, and respect your guides' instructions about where and when to step ashore.
t.sundarbans east sanctuary@21.9,89.8:
The Sundarbans are what happens when the Ganges, the Brahmaputra and the Meghna spread themselves out into the Bay of Bengal and the land simply gives up trying to be land. This is the largest mangrove forest in the world, shared between Bangladesh and India, and the part here lies in the south-west of Bangladesh, in the Khulna region, a maze of tidal channels, mud banks and islands that rise and fall with the tide. Nothing is solid for long, and there are no roads through the middle of it.

The forest takes its name, many say, from the sundari tree, whose roots send up little breathing spikes through the mud. It is the home of the Bengal tiger, which swims between islands and is said to be unusually willing to attack people, and the forest also shelters spotted deer, wild boar, saltwater crocodiles, river dolphins, and enormous numbers of birds, from kingfishers to herons. The sanctuaries here are a World Heritage site, and the trees have a practical job as well: they soak up storm surges, which is why villages behind the forest fared better in cyclones such as Sidr in 2007.

Riding here means riding to the edge. The roads on the Bangladeshi side run along flat, low-lying farmland, with shrimp ponds, rice paddies and tidal creeks, and traffic that is dense and unpredictable, a mix of buses, rickshaws, trucks, cattle and people. Surface quality changes from one village to the next, and ferry crossings are part of the journey, so allow far more time than the distance suggests. The dry season, from about November to February, is cooler and clearer, while the monsoon brings flooded roads and rough water.

Fuel and supplies are best found in the larger towns, Khulna and the port town of Mongla, before you head south, and from there the forest is explored by boat with a licensed guide and a permit from the forest department, not by bike. On the way, the old mosque city of Bagerhat is worth the detour. Its sixty-dome mosque, built in the fifteenth century under the governor Khan Jahan Ali, is the most remarkable building in the region.
t.historic mosque city of bagerhat@22.7,89:
Bagerhat is a place that makes you stop and wonder how a city of mosques ended up in the swamps of the Ganges delta. In the fifteenth century, a Muslim general and saint named Khan Jahan Ali came to this region, cleared the forest, dug ponds and roads and built a settlement that he called Khalifatabad. The brick mosques, tombs and bridges he and his followers built still stand, and UNESCO listed the site in 1985.

The most famous building is the Shait Gumbad Mosque, the Sixty Dome Mosque, though it actually has eighty-one, seventy-seven of them small and squat across the roof. Its thick brick walls, terracotta decoration and dark, cool interior make it one of the most atmospheric buildings in Bangladesh. The tomb of Khan Jahan Ali himself stands a short distance away beside a large pond full of crocodiles, which locals say are descended from the saint's own, and which visitors are asked not to disturb. The style is distinctive, with curved cornices that imitate the thatched roofs of Bengal, and it shows how Islamic architecture adapted to a wet, green climate.

The landscape is flat, humid and full of water. Rice paddies, ponds, palms and bamboo groves fill the horizon, and the Sundarbans mangrove forest, home of the Bengal tiger, is a few hours to the south. The heat is heavy and the air is damp, and the monsoon, from June to September, brings flooding and heavy rain. The best time to visit is the dry season, from November to February, when mornings are cool and the sky is clear.

Riding in Bangladesh needs patience. The roads are crowded with buses, trucks, rickshaws, bicycles and people, and the driving style is bold. On the route from Dhaka, the opening of the Padma Bridge in 2022 removed the old ferry crossing and made the trip far quicker, but it is still a long day. Bagerhat is a large town with fuel and plenty of food, with hearty curries and fresh fish. Take your shoes off at the mosque, and dress modestly.
